title: Performance Metrics & Benchmarking
summary: Why clock speed alone never settles a performance comparison, and the metrics and benchmarks that actually do the job.

slides.sectionTitle: Clock speed isn't the whole story
slides.subTitle: CPI and instruction count matter equally
slides.markdown:
A higher clock speed means each cycle is shorter, but total execution time also depends on **how many instructions** run and **how many cycles each one takes on average** (CPI — cycles per instruction). A CPU clocked lower can still finish faster if it needs fewer instructions or fewer cycles per instruction.

This is why "CPU A runs at 4 GHz, CPU B at 3 GHz, so A is faster" is not a valid conclusion on its own — clock speed is only one of three multiplied factors that determine real execution time.

slides.subTitle: Time = Instructions x CPI x Clock period
slides.markdown:
`Execution time = Instruction count x CPI x Clock period` (clock period = 1/clock speed). All three factors can move independently: a compiler can change instruction count, a microarchitecture can change CPI, and process/design choices change clock period.

A CPU with a faster clock but higher CPI, or an ISA that needs more instructions per task, can easily lose to a "slower" CPU that wins on the other two terms — the equation is the only rigorous way to compare them, term by term.

slides.subTitle: What they measure, and why they mislead
slides.markdown:
**MIPS** (millions of instructions per second) and **FLOPS** (floating-point ops per second) both try to compress performance into one number. Both fail to account for what an "instruction" or "operation" actually accomplishes across ISAs — a CISC instruction doing the work of three RISC instructions makes raw MIPS comparisons meaningless between them.

FLOPS is more meaningful within dense numerical/scientific compute, but says nothing about a workload dominated by branching, memory access, or integer logic — which is most real software.

slides.subTitle: Standardized workloads
slides.markdown:
Because raw metrics like MIPS/FLOPS mislead, the industry compares real systems using **benchmark suites** (SPEC CPU being the classic example) — a curated set of representative programs run end to end, with results reported relative to a reference machine.

The point isn't any single program's score; it's that a broad, standardized suite is much harder to game or misrepresent than a synthetic microbenchmark, and it reflects a spread of real workload types (compilers, compression, scientific code) rather than one narrow case.

slides.subTitle: Applying the performance equation
slides.markdown:
```text
Design A: 2.0 billion instructions, CPI = 1.2, clock = 3 GHz
Design B: 1.6 billion instructions, CPI = 1.5, clock = 3.5 GHz

Time_A = 2.0e9 x 1.2 / 3.0e9  = 0.80 s
Time_B = 1.6e9 x 1.5 / 3.5e9  = 0.686 s

Design B wins, despite a higher CPI, because it needs fewer
instructions and a faster clock period more than makes up for it.
```

No single factor (clock speed, CPI, or instruction count alone) predicts the winner here — only multiplying all three together does.

slides.subTitle: "Benchmarketing"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A higher benchmark score always means better real-world performance for my workload."

**Why it's wrong:** vendors sometimes tune hardware or compilers to excel at a well-known benchmark's exact code paths — nicknamed **benchmarketing** — without that tuning generalizing elsewhere. A chip that tops a chart can still underperform on a workload the benchmark doesn't represent well.

**Correct model:** treat benchmark scores as one data point, and where possible measure your **actual** workload — the only number answering "will this be faster for what I run."

slides.subTitle: Clock speed across architectures
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This CPU has a higher GHz number, so it's the faster chip."

**Why it's wrong:** clock speed comparisons are only meaningful **within the same microarchitecture and ISA**. Across different designs, a lower-clocked CPU with a lower CPI or more efficient ISA can easily outperform a higher-clocked one — exactly what happened when some architectures shifted to "more work per cycle" over raw clock speed.

**Correct model:** compare using the full performance equation or real benchmarks, never GHz alone, across chip families.
